entries.9d685abe3eec967ab4cc83a607504a9d8490d9df: <div sID="gen4312" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Josh.10" sID="Josh.10"/> <div eID="gen4312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4314" type="x-p"/> We have in this chapter an account of the conquest of the kings and kingdoms of the southern part of the land of Canaan, as, in the next chapter, of the reduction of the northern parts, which together completed the glorious successes of the wars of Canaan. In this chapter we have an account, I. Of the routing of their forces in the field, in which observe, 1. Their confederacy against the Gibeonites, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.1-Josh.10.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. 2. The Gibeonites' request to Joshua to assist them, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.6">ver. 6</reference>. 3. Joshua's speeds march under divine encouragement for their relief, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.7-Josh.10.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. 4. The defeat of the armies of these confederate kings, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.10-Josh.10.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. 5. The miraculous prolonging of the day by the standing still of the sun in favour of the conquerors, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.12-Josh.10.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. II. Of the execution of the kings that escaped out of the battle, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.15-Josh.10.27">ver. 15-27</reference>. III. Of the taking of the particular cities, and the total destruction of all that were found in them. Makkedah, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.28">ver. 28</reference>. Libnah, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.29-Josh.10.30">ver. 29, 30</reference>. Lachish, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.31-Josh.10.32">ver. 31, 32</reference>, and the king of Gezer that attempted its rescue, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.33">ver. 33</reference>. Eglon, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.34-Josh.10.35">ver. 34, 35</reference>. Hebron, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.36-Josh.10.37">ver. 36, 37</reference>. Debir, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.38-Josh.10.39">ver. 38, 39</reference>. And the bringing of all that country into the hands of Israel, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.40-Josh.10.42">ver. 40-42</reference>. And, lastly, the return of the army to the head-quarters, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.43">ver. 43</reference>.
entries.8e0c4e2301bee527e5a16fee54a4587a6e030e4e: <div eID="gen4314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4313" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Combination Against Gibeon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1450.)</title> <div sID="gen4315" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now it came to pass, when Adoni-zedec king of Jerusalem had heard how Joshua had taken Ai, and had utterly destroyed it; as he had done to Jericho and her king, so he had done to Ai and her king; and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel, and were among them; <hi type="super">2</hi> That they feared greatly, because Gibeon <hi type="italic">was</hi> a great city, as one of the royal cities, and because it <hi type="italic">was</hi> greater than Ai, and all the men thereof <hi type="italic">were</hi> mighty. <hi type="super">3</hi> Wherefore Adoni-zedec king of Jerusalem sent unto Hoham king of Hebron, and unto Piram king of Jarmuth, and unto Japhia king of Lachish, and unto Debir king of Eglon, saying, <hi type="super">4</hi> Come up unto me, and help me, that we may smite Gibeon: for it hath made peace with Joshua and with the children of Israel. <hi type="super">5</hi> Therefore the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, the king of Eglon, gathered themselves together, and went up, they and all their hosts, and encamped before Gibeon, and made war against it. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the men of Gibeon sent unto Joshua to the camp to Gilgal, saying, Slack not thy hand from thy servants; come up to us quickly, and save us, and help us: for all the kings of the Amorites that dwell in the mountains are gathered together against us. <div eID="gen4315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4316" type="x-p"/> Joshua and the hosts of Israel had now been a good while in the land of Canaan, and no great matters were effected; they were made masters of Jericho by a miracle, of Ai by stratagem, and of Gibeon by surrender, and that was all; hitherto the progress of their victories had not seemed proportionable to the magnificence of their entry and the glory of their beginnings. Those among them that were impatient of delays, it is probable, complained of Joshua's slowness, and asked why they did not immediately penetrate into the heart of the country, before the enemy could rally their forces to make head against them, why they stood trifling, while they were so confident both of their title and of their success. Thus Joshua's prudence, perhaps, was censured as slothfulness, cowardice, and want of spirit. But, 1. Canaan was not to be conquered in a day. God had said that <hi type="italic">by little and little</hi> he would drive out the Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.30">Exod. xxiii. 30</reference>. He that believeth will not make haste, or conclude that the promise will never be performed because it is not performed so soon as he expected. 2. Joshua waited for the Canaanites to be the aggressors; let them first make an onset upon Israel, or the allies of Israel, and then their destruction will be, or at least will appear to be, the more just and more justifiable. Joshua had warrant sufficient to set upon them, yet he stays till they strike the first stroke, that he might provide for honest things in the sight, not only of God, but of men; and they would be the more inexcusable in their resistance, now that they had seen what favour the Gibeonites found with Israel. 3. It was for the advantage of Israel to sit still awhile, that the forces of these little kings might unite in one body, and so might the more easily be cut off at one blow. This God had in his eye when he put it into their hearts to combine against Israel; though they designed thereby to strengthen one another, that which he intended was to gather them as sheaves into the floor, to fall together under the flail, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.12">Mic. iv. 12</reference>. Thus oftentimes that seeming paradox proves wholesome counsel, <hi type="italic">Stay awhile, and we shall have done the sooner.</hi> <div eID="gen4316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4317" type="x-p"/> After Israel had waited awhile for an occasion to make war upon the Canaanites, a fair one offers itself. 1. Five kings combine against the Gibeonites. Adoni-zedec king of Jerusalem was the first mover and ring-leader of this confederacy. He had a good name (it signifies <hi type="italic">lord of righteousness</hi>), being a descendant perhaps from Melchizedek, <hi type="italic">king of righteousness;</hi> but, notwithstanding the goodness of his name and family, it seems he was a bad man, and an implacable enemy to the posterity of that Abraham to whom his predecessor, Melchizedek, was such a faithful friend. He called upon his neighbours to join against Israel either because he was the most honourable prince, and had the precedency among these kings (perhaps they had some dependence upon him, at least they paid a deference to him, as the most public, powerful, and active man they had among them), or because he was first or most apprehensive of the danger his country was in, not only by the conquest of Jericho and Ai, but the surrender of Gibeon, which, it seems, was the chief thing that alarmed him, it being one of the most considerable frontier towns they had. Against Gibeon therefore all the force he would raise must be leveled. <hi type="italic">Come,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">and help me, that we may smite Gibeon.</hi> This he resolves to do, either, (1.) In policy, that he might retake the city, because it was a strong city, and of great consequence to this country in whose hands it was; or, (2.) In passion, that he might chastise the citizens for making peace with Joshua, pretending that they had perfidiously betrayed their country and strengthened the common enemy, whereas they had really done the greatest kindness imaginable to their country, by setting them a good example, if they would have followed it. Thus Satan and his instruments make war upon those that make peace with God. <hi type="italic">Marvel not if the world hate you,</hi> and treat those as deserters who are converts to Christ. 2. The Gibeonites send notice to Joshua of the distress and danger they are in, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.6">v. 6</reference>. Now they expect benefit from the league they had made with Israel, because, though it was obtained by deceit, it was afterwards confirmed when the truth came out. They think Joshua obliged to help them, (1.) In conscience, because they were his servants; not in compliment, as they had said in their first address (<reference osisRef="Josh.9.8">ch. ix. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">We are thy servants,</hi> but in reality made servants to the congregation; and it is the duty of masters to take care of the poorest and meanest of their servants, and not to see them wronged when it is in the power of their hand to right them. Those that pay allegiance may reasonably expect protection. Thus David pleads with God (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.94">Ps. cxix. 94</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am thine, save me;</hi> and so may we, if indeed we be his. (2.) In honour, because the ground of their enemies' quarrel with them was the respect they had shown to Israel, and the confidence they had in a covenant with them. Joshua cannot refuse to help them when it is for their affection to him, and to the name of his God, that they are attacked. David thinks it a good plea with God (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.7">Ps. lxix. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">For thy sake I have borne reproach.</hi> When our spiritual enemies set themselves in array against us, and threaten to swallow us up, let us, by faith and prayer, apply to Christ, our Joshua, for strength and succour, as Paul did, and we shall receive the same answer of peace, <hi type="italic">My grace is sufficient for thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.8-2Cor.12.9">2 Cor. xii. 8, 9</reference>.
entries.2b59cc237aad3563ae711e27f178ab7400343667: <div eID="gen4317" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sun and Moon Stand Still. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1450.)</title> <div sID="gen4318" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> So Joshua ascended from Gilgal, he, and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valour. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Joshua, Fear them not: for I have delivered them into thine hand; there shall not a man of them stand before thee. <hi type="super">9</hi> Joshua therefore came unto them suddenly, <hi type="italic">and</hi> went up from Gilgal all night. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> discomfited them before Israel, and slew them with a great slaughter at Gibeon, and chased them along the way that goeth up to Beth-horon, and smote them to Azekah, and unto Makkedah. <hi type="super">11</hi> And it came to pass, as they fled from before Israel, <hi type="italic">and</hi> were in the going down to Beth-horon, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> cast down great stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and they died: <hi type="italic">they were</hi> more which died with hailstones than <hi type="italic">they</hi> whom the children of Israel slew with the sword. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then spake Joshua to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the day when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delivered up the Amorites before the children of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day. <hi type="super">14</hi> And there was no day like that before it or after it, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hearkened unto the voice of a man: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> fought for Israel. <div eID="gen4318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4319" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Joshua resolves to assist the Gibeonites, and God encourages him in this resolve. 1. He ascended from Gilgal (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.7">v. 7</reference>), that is, he designed, determined, and prepared for, this expedition to relieve Gibeon, for it is probable it was before he stirred a step that God spoke to him to encourage him. It was generous and just in Joshua to help his new allies, though perhaps the king of Jerusalem, when he attacked them, little thought that Joshua would be so ready to help them, but expected he would abandon them as Canaanites, the rather because they had obtained their league with him by fraud; therefore he speaks with assurance (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.4">v. 4</reference>) of smiting Gibeon. But Joshua knew that his promise to let them live obliged him, not only not to slay them himself, but not to stand by and see them slain when it was in the power of his hand to prevent it, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.11-Prov.24.12">Prov. xxiv. 11, 12</reference>. He knew that when they embraced the faith and worship of the God of Israel they came to trust under the shadow of his wings (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.12">Ruth ii. 12</reference>), and therefore, as his servants, he was bound to protect them. 2. God animated him for his undertaking, (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fear not,</hi> that is, (1.) "Doubt not of the goodness of thy cause and the clearness of thy call; though it be to assist Gibeonites, thou art in the way of duty, and God is with thee of a truth." (2.) "Dread not the power of the enemy; though so many kings are confederate against thee, and are resolved to make their utmost efforts for the reduction of Gibeon, and it may be will fight desperately in a desperate cause, yet let not this discourage thee, <hi type="italic">I have delivered them into thy hand;</hi>" and those can make neither resistance nor escape whom God has marked for destruction. <div eID="gen4319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4320" type="x-p"/> II. Joshua applies himself to execute this resolve, and God assists him in the execution. Here we have, <div eID="gen4320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4321" type="x-p"/> 1. The great industry of Joshua, and the power of God working with it for the defeat of the enemy. In this action, (1.) Joshua showed his good-will in the haste he made for the relief of Gibeon (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">He came unto them suddenly,</hi> for the extremity was such as would not admit delay. If one of the tribes of Israel had been in danger, he could not have shown more care or zeal for its relief than here for Gibeon, remembering in this, as in other cases, there must be one law for the stranger that was proselyted and for him that was born in the land. Scarcely had the confederate princes got their forces together, and sat down before Gibeon, when Joshua was upon them, the surprise of which would put them into the greatest confusion. Now that the enemy were actually drawn up into a body, which had all as it were but one neck, despatch was as serviceable to his cause as before delay was, while he waited for this general rendezvous; and now that things were ripe for execution no man more expeditious than Joshua, who before had seemed slow. Now it shall never be said, <hi type="italic">He left that to be done to-morrow which he could do to-day.</hi> When Joshua found he could not reach Gibeon in a day, lest he should lose any real advantages against the enemy, or so much as seem to come short or to neglect his new allies, he marched all night, resolving not to give sleep to his eyes, nor slumber to his eye-lids, till he had accomplished this enterprise. It was well the forces he took with him were mighty men of valour, not only able-bodied men, but men of spirit and resolution, and hearty in the cause, else they neither could nor would have borne this fatigue, but would have murmured at their leader and would have asked, "Is this the rest we were promised in Canaan?" But they well considered that the present toil was in order to a happy settlement, and therefore were reconciled to it. Let the <hi type="italic">good soldiers of Jesus Christ</hi> learn hence to <hi type="italic">endure hardness, in following the Lamb whithersoever he goes,</hi> and not think themselves undone if their religion lose them now and then a night's sleep; it will be enough to rest when we come to heaven. But why needed Joshua to put himself and his men so much to the stretch? Had not God promised him that without fail he would <hi type="italic">deliver the enemies into his hand?</hi> It is true he had; but God's promises are intended, not to slacken and supersede, but to quicken and encourage our endeavours. He that believeth doth not make haste to anticipate providence, but doth make haste to attend it, with a diligent, not a distrustful, speed. (2.) God showed his great power in defeating the enemies whom Joshua so vigorously attacked, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.10-Josh.10.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Joshua had a very numerous and powerful army with him, hands enough to despatch a dispirited enemy, so that the enemy might have been scattered by the ordinary fate of war; but God himself would appear in this great and decisive battle, and draw up the artillery of heaven against the Canaanites, to demonstrate to this people that they <hi type="italic">got not this land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them, but God's right hand and his arm,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">Ps. xliv. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord discomfited them before Israel.</hi> Israel did what they could, and yet God did all. [1.] It must needs be a very great terror and confusion to the enemy to perceive that heaven itself fought against them; for who can contest with, flee from, or fence against, the powers of heaven? They had affronted the true God and robbed him of his honour by worshipping the host of heaven, giving that worship to the creature which is due to the Creator only; and now the host of heaven fights against them, and even that part of the creation which they had idolized is at war with them, and even triumphs in their ruin, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.2">Jer. viii. 2</reference>. There is no way of making any creature propitious to us, no, not by sacrifice nor offering, but only by making our peace with God and keeping ourselves in his love. This had been enough to make them an easy prey to the victorious Israelites, yet this was not all. [2.] Besides the terror struck upon them, there was a great slaughter made of them by hail-stones, which were so large, and came down with such a force, that more were killed by the hail-stones than by the sword of the Israelites, though no doubt they were busy. God himself speaks to Job of treasures, or magazines, of snow and hail, which he has <hi type="italic">reserved for the day of battle and war</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.22-Job.38.23">Job xxxviii. 22, 23</reference>), and here they are made use of to destroy the Canaanites. Here was hail, shot from God's great ordnance, that, against whomsoever it was directed, was sure to hit (and never glanced upon the Israelites mixed with them), and wherever it hit was sure to kill. See here how miserable those are that have God for their enemy, and how sure to perish; it is a fearful thing to fall into his hands, for there is no fleeing out of them. Some observe that Beth-horon lay north of Gibeon, Azekah and Makkedah lay south, so that they fled each way but, which way soever they fled, the hail-stones pursued them, and met them at every turn. <div eID="gen4321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4322" type="x-p"/> 2. The great faith of Joshua, and the power of God crowning it with the miraculous arrest of the sun, that the day of Israel's victories might be prolonged, and so the enemy totally defeated. The hail-stones had their rise no higher than the clouds, but, to show that Israel's help came from above the clouds, the sun itself, who by his constant motion serves the whole earth, by halting when there was occasion served the Israelites, and did them a kindness. <hi type="italic">The sun and moon stood still in their habitation, at the light of thy arrows</hi> which gave the signal, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.11">Hab. iii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen4322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4323" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is the prayer of Joshua that the sun might stand still. I call it his prayer, because it is said (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.12">v. 12</reference>) <hi type="italic">he spoke to the Lord;</hi> as Elijah, though we read (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.1">1 Kings xvii. 1</reference>) only of his prophesying of the drought, yet is said (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.17">James v. 17</reference>) to pray for it. Observe, [1.] An instance of Joshua's unwearied activity in the service of God and Israel, that though he had marched all night and fought all day, and, one might expect, would be inclined to repose himself and get a little sleep, and give his army some time to rest—that, like the hireling, he would earnestly desire the shadow, and bid the night welcome, when he had done such a good day's work—yet, instead of this, he wishes for nothing so much as the prolonging of the day. Note, Those that <hi type="italic">wait on the Lord</hi> and work for him <hi type="italic">shall renew their strength, shall run and not be weary, shall walk and not faint,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa. xl. 31</reference>. [2.] An instance of his great faith in the almighty power of God, as above the power of nature, and able to control and alter the usual course of it. No doubt Joshua had an extraordinary impulse or impression upon his spirit, which he knew to be of divine origin, prompting him to desire that this miracle might be wrought upon this occasion, else it would have been presumption in him to desire or expect; the prayer would not have been granted by the divine power, if it had not been dictated by the divine grace. God wrought this faith in him, and then said, "<hi type="italic">According to thy faith,</hi> and thy prayer of faith, <hi type="italic">be it unto thee.</hi>" It cannot be imagined, however, that such a thing as this should have entered into his mind if God had not put it there; a man would have had a thousand projects in his head for the completing of the victory before he would have thought of desiring the sun to stand still; but even in the Old-Testament saints <hi type="italic">the Spirit made intercession according to the will of God.</hi> What God will give he inclines the hearts of his praying people to ask, and for what he will do he will be enquired of, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.37">Ezek. xxxvi. 37</reference>. Now, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It looked great for Joshua to say, <hi type="italic">Sun, stand thou still.</hi> His ancestor Joseph had indeed dreamed that the sun and moon did homage to him; but who would have thought that, after it had been fulfilled in the figure, it should be again fulfilled in the letter to one of his posterity? The prayer is thus expressed with authority, because it was not an ordinary prayer, such as is directed and supported only by God's common providence or promise, but the prayer of a prophet at this time divinely inspired for this purpose; and yet it intimates to us the prevalency of prayer in general, so far as it is regulated by the word of God, and may remind us of that honour put upon prayer (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.11">Isa. xlv. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Concerning the work of my hands command you me.</hi> He bids the sun stand still upon Gibeon, the place of action and the seat of war, intimating that what he designed in this request was the advantage of Israel against their enemies; it is probable that the sun was now declining, and that he did not call for the lengthening out of the day until he observed it hastening towards it period. He does likewise, in the name of the King of kings, arrest the moon, perhaps because it was requisite for the preserving of the harmony and good order of the spheres that the course of the rest of the heavenly bodies should be stayed likewise, otherwise, while the sun shone, he needed not the moon; and here he mentions the valley of Ajalon, which was near to Gibeon, because there he was at that time. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It was bold indeed to say so before Israel, and argues a very strong assurance of faith. If the event had not answered the demand, nothing could have been a greater slur upon him; the Israelites would have concluded he was certainly going mad, or he would never have talked so extravagantly. But he knew very well God would own and answer a petition which he himself directed to be drawn up and presented, and therefore was not afraid to say before all Israel, calling them to observe this work of wonder, <hi type="italic">Sun, stand thou still,</hi> for he was confident in him whom he had trusted. He believed the almighty power of God, else he could not have expected that the sun, going on in its strength, driving in a full career, and <hi type="italic">rejoicing as a strong man to run a race,</hi> should be stopped in an instant. He believed the sovereignty of God in the kingdom of nature, else he could not have expected that the established law and course of nature should be changed and interrupted, the ordinances of heaven, and the constant usage according to these ordinances, broken in upon. And he believed God's particular favour to Israel above all people under the sun, else he could not have expected that, to favour them upon an emergency with a double day, he should (which must follow of course) amaze and terrify so great a part of the terrestrial globe with a double night at the same time. It is true, he <hi type="italic">causeth the sun to shine upon the just and the unjust;</hi> but for this once the unjust shall wait for it beyond the usual time, while, in favour to righteous Israel, it stands still. <div eID="gen4323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4324" type="x-p"/> (2.) The wonderful answer to this prayer. No sooner said than done (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sun stood still, and the moon staid.</hi> Notwithstanding the vast distance between the earth and the sun, at the word of Joshua the sun stopped immediately; for the same God that rules in heaven above rules at the same time on this earth, and, when he pleases, even <hi type="italic">the heavens shall hear the earth,</hi> as here. Concerning this great miracle it is here said, [1.] <hi type="italic">That it continued a whole day,</hi> that is, the sun continued as long again above the horizon as otherwise it would have done. It is commonly supposed to have been about the middle of summer that this happened, when, in that country, it was about fourteen hours between sun and sun, so that this day was about twenty-eight hours long; yet, if we suppose it to have been at that time of the year when the days are at the shortest, it will be the more probable that Joshua should desire and pray for the prolonging of the day. [2.] That hereby the people had full time to avenge themselves of their enemies, and to give them a total defeat. We often read in history of battles which the night put an end to, the shadows of which favoured the retreat of the conquered; to prevent this advantage to the enemy in their flight, the day was doubled, that the hand of Israel might <hi type="italic">find out all their enemies;</hi> but the eye and hand of God can find them out without the help of the sun's light, for to him <hi type="italic">the night shineth as the day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.139.12">Ps. cxxxix. 12</reference>. Note, Sometimes God completes a great salvation in a little time, and makes but one day's work of it. Perhaps this miracle is alluded to <reference osisRef="Zech.14.6-Zech.14.7">Zech. xiv. 6, 7</reference>, where the day of God's fighting against the nations is said to be <hi type="italic">one day,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">at evening time it shall be light,</hi> as here. And, [3.] That there was <hi type="italic">never any day like it,</hi> before or since, in which God put such an honour upon faith and prayer, and upon Israel's cause; never did he so wonderfully comply with the request of a man, nor so wonderfully fight for his people. [4.] This is said to be written <hi type="italic">in the book of Jasher,</hi> a collection of state-poems, in which the poem made upon this occasion was preserved among the rest; probably the same with that <hi type="italic">book of the wars of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.21.14">Num. xxi. 14</reference>), which afterwards was continued and carried on by one Jasher. Those words, <hi type="italic">Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon, and thou moon in the valley of Ajalon,</hi> sounding metrical, are supposed to be taken from the narrative of this event as it was found in the book of Jasher. Not that the divine testimony of the book of Joshua needed confirmation from the book of Jasher, a human composition; but to those who had that book in their hands it would be of use to compare this history with it, which warrants the appeals the learned make to profane history for corroborating the proofs of the truth of sacred history. [5.] But surely this stupendous miracle of the standing still of the sun was intended for something more than merely to give Israel so much the more time to find out and kill their enemies, which, without this, might have been done the next day. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God would hereby magnify Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.7">ch. iii. 7</reference>), as a particular favourite, and one whom he did delight to honour, being a type of him who has all power both in heaven and in earth and whom the winds and the seas obey. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He would hereby notify to all the world what he was doing for his people Israel here in Canaan; the sun, the eye of the world, must be fixed for some hours upon Gibeon and the valley of Ajalon, as if to contemplate the great works of God there for Israel, and so to engage the children of men to look that way, and to <hi type="italic">enquire of this wonder done in the land,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2 Chron. xxxii. 31</reference>. Proclamation was hereby made to all the neighbouring nations. <hi type="italic">Come, behold the works of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.8">Ps. xlvi. 8</reference>), and say, <hi type="italic">What nation is there so great as Israel is, who has God so nigh unto them?</hi> One would have supposed that this would bring such real ambassadors as the Gibeonites pretended to be from a very far country, to court the friendship of Israel because of the name of the Lord their God. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He would hereby convince and confound those idolaters that worshipped the sun and moon and gave divine honours to them, by demonstrating that they were subject to the command of the God of Israel, and that, as high as they were, he was above them; and thus he would fortify his people against temptations to this idolatry, which he foresaw they would be addicted to (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">Deut. iv. 19</reference>), and which, notwithstanding this, they afterwards corrupted themselves with. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> This miracle signified (it is the learned bishop Pierson's notion) that in the latter days, when the light of the world was tending towards a light of darkness, the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness,</hi> even our Joshua, should arise (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.2">Mal. iv. 2</reference>), give check to the approaching night, and be the true light. To which let me add that when Christ conquered our spiritual enemies upon the cross the miracle wrought on the sun was the reverse of this; it was then darkened as if it had gone down at noon, for Christ needed not the light of the sun to carry on his victories: he then made darkness his pavilion. And, <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The arresting of the sun and moon in this day of battle prefigured the turning of the sun into darkness, and the moon into blood, in the last great and terrible day of the Lord.
entries.6c5388e0f84c42a1105aa5cdb31fc7d65295f880: <div eID="gen4324" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Five Kings Slain. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1450.)</title> <div sID="gen4325" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, unto the camp to Gilgal. <hi type="super">16</hi> But these five kings fled, and hid themselves in a cave at Makkedah. <hi type="super">17</hi> And it was told Joshua, saying, The five kings are found hid in a cave at Makkedah. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Joshua said, Roll great stones upon the mouth of the cave, and set men by it for to keep them: <hi type="super">19</hi> And stay ye not, <hi type="italic">but</hi> pursue after your enemies, and smite the hindmost of them; suffer them not to enter into their cities: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God hath delivered them into your hand. <hi type="super">20</hi> And it came to pass, when Joshua and the children of Israel had made an end of slaying them with a very great slaughter, till they were consumed, that the rest <hi type="italic">which</hi> remained of them entered into fenced cities. <hi type="super">21</hi> And all the people returned to the camp to Joshua at Makkedah in peace: none moved his tongue against any of the children of Israel. <hi type="super">22</hi> Then said Joshua, Open the mouth of the cave, and bring out those five kings unto me out of the cave. <hi type="super">23</hi> And they did so, and brought forth those five kings unto him out of the cave, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the king of Eglon. <hi type="super">24</hi> And it came to pass, when they brought out those kings unto Joshua, that Joshua called for all the men of Israel, and said unto the captains of the men of war which went with him, Come near, put your feet upon the necks of these kings. And they came near, and put their feet upon the necks of them. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Joshua said unto them, Fear not, nor be dismayed, be strong and of good courage: for thus shall the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> do to all your enemies against whom ye fight. <hi type="super">26</hi> And afterward Joshua smote them, and slew them, and hanged them on five trees: and they were hanging upon the trees until the evening. <hi type="super">27</hi> And it came to pass at the time of the going down of the sun, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Joshua commanded, and they took them down off the trees, and cast them into the cave wherein they had been hid, and laid great stones in the cave's mouth, <hi type="italic">which remain</hi> until this very day. <div eID="gen4325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4326" type="x-p"/> It was a brave appearance, no doubt, which the five kings made when they took the field for the reducing of Gibeon, and a brave army they had following them; but they were all routed, put into disorder first, and then brought to destruction by the hail-stones. And now Joshua thought, his work being done, he might go with his army into quarters of refreshment. Accordingly it was resolved, perhaps in a council of war, that they should presently return <hi type="italic">to the camp at Gilgal</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.15">v. 15</reference>), till they should receive orders from God to take possession of the country they had now conquered; but he soon finds he has more work cut out for him. The victory must be pursued, that the spoils might be divided. Accordingly he applies himself to it with renewed vigour. <div eID="gen4326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4327" type="x-p"/> I. The forces that had dispersed themselves must be followed and smitten. When tidings were brought to Joshua where the kings were he ordered a guard to be set upon them for the present (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.18">v. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">reserving them</hi> for another <hi type="italic">day of destruction,</hi> and to be <hi type="italic">brought forth to a day of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job xxi. 30</reference>. He directs his men to pursue the common soldiers, as much as might be, to prevent their escaping to the garrisons, which would strengthen them, and make the reduction of them the more difficult, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.19">v. 19</reference>. Like a prudent general, he does that first which is most needful, and defers his triumphs till he has completed his conquests; nor was he in such haste to insult over the captive kings but that he would first prevent the rallying again of their scattered forces. The result of this vigorous pursuit was, 1. That a very great slaughter was made of the enemies of God and Israel. And, 2. The field was cleared of them, so that none remained but such as got into fenced cities, where they would not long be safe themselves, nor were they capable of doing any service to the cities that sheltered them, unless they could have left their fears behind them. 3. <hi type="italic">None moved his tongue against any of the children of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.10.21">v. 21</reference>. This expression intimates, (1.) Their perfect safety and tranquillity; some think it should be read (from <reference osisRef="Exod.11.7">Exod. xi. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Against any of the children of Israel did not a dog move his tongue;</hi> no, not against any one man of them. They were not threatened by any danger at all after their victory, no, not so much as the barking of a dog. Not one single Israelite (for the original makes it so particular) was brought into any distress, either in the battle or in the pursuit. (2.) Their honour and reputation; no man had any reproach to cast upon them, nor an ill word to give them. God not only tied the hands, but stopped the mouths, of their enraged enemies, and put lying lips to silence. (3.) The Chaldee paraphrase makes it an expression of their unalloyed joy for this victory, reading it, <hi type="italic">There was no hurt nor loss to the children of Israel, for which any man should afflict his soul.</hi> When the army came to be reviewed after the battle, there was none slain, none wounded, none missing. Not one Israelite had occasion to lament either the loss of a friend or the loss of a limb, so cheap, so easy, so glorious, was this victory. <div eID="gen4327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4328" type="x-p"/> II. The kings that had hidden themselves must now be called to an account, as rebels against the Israel of God, to whom, by the divine promise and grant, this land did of right belong and should have been surrendered upon demand. See here, <div eID="gen4328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4329" type="x-p"/> 1. How they were secured. The cave which they fled to, and trusted in for a refuge, became their prison, in which they were clapped up, till Joshua sat in judgment on them, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.18">v. 18</reference>. It seems they all escaped both the hail-stones and the sword, God so ordering it, not in kindness to them, but that they might be reserved for a more solemn and terrible execution; as, for this cause, Pharaoh survived the plagues of Egypt, and was made to stand, that God might in him <hi type="italic">show his power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.9.16">Exod. ix. 16</reference>. They all fled, and met at the same place, Providence directing them; and now those who were lately consulting against Israel were put upon new counsels to preserve themselves and agreed to take shelter in the same cave. The information brought to Joshua of this is an evidence that there were those of the country, who knew the holes and fastnesses of it, that were in his interests. And the care Joshua took to keep them there when they were there, as it is an instance of his policy and presence of mind, even in the heat of action, so, in the result of their project, it shows how those not only deceive themselves, but destroy themselves, who think to hide themselves from God. Their refuge of lies will but bind them over to God's judgment. <div eID="gen4329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4330" type="x-p"/> 2. How they were triumphed over. Joshua ordered them to be brought forth out of the cave, set before him as at the bar, and their names called over, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.22-Josh.10.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. And when they either were bound and cast upon the ground unable to help themselves, or threw themselves upon the ground, humbly to beg for their lives, he called for the general officers and great men, and commanded them to trample upon these kings, and set their feet upon their necks, not in sport and to make themselves and the company merry, but with the gravity and decorum that became the ministers of the divine justice who were not herein to gratify any pride or passion of their own, but to give glory to the God of Israel as higher than the highest, who <hi type="italic">treads upon princes as mortar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.25">Isa. xli. 25</reference>), and <hi type="italic">is terrible to the kings of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.76.12">Ps. lxxvi. 12</reference>. The thing does indeed look barbarous, thus to insult over men in misery, who had suddenly fallen from the highest pitch of honour into this disgrace. It was hard for crowned heads to be thus trodden upon, not by Joshua himself (that might better have been borne), at least not by him only, but by all the captains of the army. Certainly it ought not to be drawn into a precedent, for the case was extraordinary, and we have reason to think it was by divine direction and impulse that Joshua did this. (1.) God would hereby punish the abominable wickedness of these kings, the measure of whose iniquity was now full. And, by this public act of justice done upon these ringleaders of the Canaanites in sin, he would possess his people with the greater dread and detestation of those sins of <hi type="italic">the nations that God cast out from before them,</hi> which they would be tempted to imitate. (2.) He would hereby have the promise by Moses made good (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">Deut. xxxiii. 29</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou shalt tread upon their high places,</hi> that is, their great men, which should the rather be speedily fulfilled in the letter because they are the very last words of Moses that we find upon record. (3.) He would hereby encourage the faith and hope of his people Israel in reference to the wars that were yet before them. Therefore Joshua said (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fear not, nor be dismayed.</hi> [1.] "Fear not these kings, nor any of theirs, as if there were any danger of having this affront now put upon them in after-time revenged upon yourselves, a consideration which keeps many from being insolent towards those they have at their mercy, because they know not how soon the uncertain fate of war may turn the same wheel upon themselves; but you need not fear that any should rise up ever to revenge this quarrel." [2.] "Fear not any other kings, who may at any time be in confederacy against you, for you see these brought down, whom you thought formidable. <hi type="italic">Thus shall the Lord do to all your enemies;</hi> now that they begin to fall, to fall so low that you may set your feet on their necks, you may be confident that they shall not prevail, but shall <hi type="italic">surely fall before you,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Esth.6.13">Esth. vi. 13</reference>. (4.) He would hereby give a type and figure of Christ's victories over the powers of darkness, and believers' victories through him. All the enemies of the Redeemer shall be <hi type="italic">made his footstool,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>. And see <reference osisRef="Ps.18.40">Ps. xviii. 40</reference>. The <hi type="italic">kings of the earth set themselves</hi> against him (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Ps. ii. 2</reference>), but sooner or later we shall see all things put under Him (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.8">Heb. ii. 8</reference>), and <hi type="italic">principalities and powers</hi> made a show of, <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>. And in these triumphs we are more than conquerors, may <hi type="italic">tread upon the lion and adder</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.13">Ps. xci. 13</reference>), may <hi type="italic">ride on the high places of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">Isa. lviii. 14</reference>), and may be confident that <hi type="italic">the God of peace shall tread Satan under our feet,</hi> shall do it shortly and do it effectually, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.20">Rom. xvi. 20</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.149.8-Ps.149.9">Ps. cxlix. 8, 9</reference>. <div eID="gen4330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4331" type="x-p"/> 3. How they were put to death. Perhaps, when they had undergone that terrible mortification of being trodden upon by the captains of Israel, they were ready to say, as Agag, <hi type="italic">Surely the bitterness of death is past,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">sufficient unto them was this punishment which was inflicted by many;</hi> but their honours cannot excuse their lives, their forfeited devoted lives. Joshua smote them with the sword, and then hanged up their bodies till evening, when they were taken down, and thrown <hi type="italic">into the cave in which they had hidden themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.10.26-Josh.10.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. That which they thought would have been their shelter was made their prison first and then their grave; so shall we be disappointed in that which we flee to from God: yet to good people the grave is still <hi type="italic">a hiding-place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job xiv. 13</reference>. If these five kings had humbled themselves in time, and had begged peace instead of waging war, they might have saved their lives; but now the decree had gone forth, and they <hi type="italic">found no place for repentance,</hi> or the reversal of the judgment; it was too late to expect it, though perhaps <hi type="italic">they sought it carefully with tears.</hi>
entries.2119cf2762c0ae4d12ddb731c2857656c0366a3d: <div eID="gen4331" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Seven Kings Defeated and Slain. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1450.)</title> <div sID="gen4332" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> And that day Joshua took Makkedah, and smote it with the edge of the sword, and the king thereof he utterly destroyed, them, and all the souls that <hi type="italic">were</hi> therein; he let none remain: and he did to the king of Makkedah as he did unto the king of Jericho. <hi type="super">29</hi> Then Joshua passed from Makkedah, and all Israel with him, unto Libnah, and fought against Libnah: <hi type="super">30</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delivered it also, and the king thereof, into the hand of Israel; and he smote it with the edge of the sword, and all the souls that <hi type="italic">were</hi> therein; he let none remain in it; but did unto the king thereof as he did unto the king of Jericho. <hi type="super">31</hi> And Joshua passed from Libnah, and all Israel with him, unto Lachish, and encamped against it, and fought against it: <hi type="super">32</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delivered Lachish into the hand of Israel, which took it on the second day, and smote it with the edge of the sword, and all the souls that <hi type="italic">were</hi> therein, according to all that he had done to Libnah. <hi type="super">33</hi> Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish; and Joshua smote him and his people, until he had left him none remaining. <hi type="super">34</hi> And from Lachish Joshua passed unto Eglon, and all Israel with him; and they encamped against it, and fought against it: <hi type="super">35</hi> And they took it on that day, and smote it with the edge of the sword, and all the souls that <hi type="italic">were</hi> therein he utterly destroyed that day, according to all that he had done to Lachish. <hi type="super">36</hi> And Joshua went up from Eglon, and all Israel with him, unto Hebron; and they fought against it: <hi type="super">37</hi> And they took it, and smote it with the edge of the sword, and the king thereof, and all the cities thereof, and all the souls that <hi type="italic">were</hi> therein; he left none remaining, according to all that he had done to Eglon; but destroyed it utterly, and all the souls that <hi type="italic">were</hi> therein. <hi type="super">38</hi> And Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to Debir; and fought against it: <hi type="super">39</hi> And he took it, and the king thereof, and all the cities thereof; and they smote them with the edge of the sword, and utterly destroyed all the souls that <hi type="italic">were</hi> therein; he left none remaining: as he had done to Hebron, so he did to Debir, and to the king thereof; as he had done also to Libnah, and to her king. <hi type="super">40</hi> So Joshua smote all the country of the hills, and of the south, and of the vale, and of the springs, and all their kings: he left none remaining, but utterly destroyed all that breathed, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel commanded. <hi type="super">41</hi> And Joshua smote them from Kadesh-barnea even unto Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, even unto Gibeon. <hi type="super">42</hi> And all these kings and their land did Joshua take at one time, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel fought for Israel. <hi type="super">43</hi> And Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, unto the camp to Gilgal. <div eID="gen4332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4333" type="x-p"/> We are here informed how Joshua improved the late glorious victory he had obtained and the advantages he had gained by it, and to do this well is a general's praise. <div eID="gen4333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4334" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a particular account of the several cities which he immediately made himself master of. 1. The cities of three of the kings whom he had conquered in the field he went and took possession of, Lachish (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.31-Josh.10.32">v. 31, 32</reference>), Eglon (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.34-Josh.10.35">v. 34, 35</reference>), and Hebron, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.36-Josh.10.37">v. 36, 37</reference>. The other two, Jerusalem and Jarmuth, were not taken at this time; perhaps his forces were either so much fatigued with what they had done or so well content with what they had got that they had no mind to attack those places, and so they let slip the fairest opportunity they could ever expect of reducing them with ease, which afterwards was not done without difficulty, <reference osisRef="Judg.1.8">Judg. i. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.6">2 Sam. v. 6</reference>. 2. Three other cities, and royal cities too, he took: Makkedah, into the neighbourhood of which the five kings had fled, which brought Joshua and his forces thither in pursuit of them, and so hastened its ruin (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.28">v. 28</reference>), Libnah (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.29-Josh.10.30">v. 29, 30</reference>), and Debir, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.38-Josh.10.39">v. 38, 39</reference>. 3. One king that brought in his forces for the relief of Lachish, that had lost its king, proved to meddle to his own hurt; it was Horam king of Gezer, who, either in friendship to his neighbours or for his own security, offered to stop the progress of Joshua's arms, and was cut off with all his forces, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.33">v. 33</reference>. Thus wicked men are often snared in their counsels, and, by opposing God in the way of his judgments, bring them the sooner on their own heads. <div eID="gen4334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4335" type="x-p"/> II. A general account of the country which was hereby reduced and brought into Israel's hands (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.40-Josh.10.42">v. 40-42</reference>), that part of the land of Canaan of which they first got possession, which lay south of Jerusalem, and afterwards fell, for the most part, to the lot of the tribe of Judah. Observe in this narrative, <div eID="gen4335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4336" type="x-p"/> 1. The great speed Joshua made in taking these cities, which, some think, is intimated in the manner of relating it, which is quick and concise. He flew like lightning from place to place; and though they all stood it out to the last extremity, and none of these cities opened their gates to him, yet in a little time he got them all into his hands, summoned them, and seized them, the same day (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.28">v. 28</reference>), or in two days, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.32">v. 32</reference>. Now that they were struck with fear, by the defeat of their armies and the death of their kings, Joshua prudently followed his blow. See what a great deal of work may be done in a little time, if we will but be busy and improve our opportunities. <div eID="gen4336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4337" type="x-p"/> 2. The great severity Joshua used towards those he conquered. He gave no quarter to man, woman, nor child, put to the sword <hi type="italic">all the souls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.28">v. 28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.30">30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.32">32,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.35">35</reference>, &c.), <hi type="italic">utterly destroyed all that breathed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.40">v. 40</reference>), and <hi type="italic">left none remaining.</hi> Nothing could justify this military execution but that herein they did <hi type="italic">as the Lord God of Israel commanded</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.40">v. 40</reference>), which was sufficient not only to bear them out, and save them for the imputation of cruelty, but to sanctify what they did, and make it an acceptable piece of service to his justice. God would hereby, (1.) Manifest his hatred of the idolatries and other abominations which the Canaanites had been guilty of, and leave us to judge how great the provocation was which they had given him by the greatness of the destruction which was brought upon them when the measure of their iniquity was full. (2.) He would hereby magnify his love to his people Israel, in giving so many men for them, and <hi type="italic">people for their life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 4</reference>. When the <hi type="italic">heathen are to be cast out to make room for this vine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.8">Ps. lxxx. 8</reference>) divine justice appears more prodigal than ever of human blood, that the Israelites might find themselves for ever obliged to spend their lives to the glory of that God who had sacrificed so many of the lives of his creatures to their interest. (3.) Hereby was typified the final and eternal destruction of all the impenitent implacable enemies of the Lord Jesus, who, having slighted the riches of his grace, must for ever feel the weight of his wrath, and shall <hi type="italic">have judgment without mercy. Nations that forget God shall be turned into hell,</hi> and no reproach at all to God's infinite goodness. <div eID="gen4337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4338" type="x-p"/> 3. The great success of this expedition. The spoil of these cities was now divided among the men of war that plundered them; and the cities themselves, with the land about them, were shortly to be divided among the tribes, for the Lord <hi type="italic">fought for Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.10.42">v. 42</reference>. They could not have gotten the victory if God had not undertaken the battle; then we conquer when God fights for us; and, <hi type="italic">if he be for us, who can be against us?</hi>  <chapter eID="Josh.10"/> <div eID="gen4338" type="x-p"/>

entries.86ee80912181a54dbebe52ed2525d30d6cefcf40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2079"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.10.1-Josh.10.5">Jos 10:1-5</reference>. Five Kings War against Gibeon.</title> <div sID="gen2782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2079"/><hi type="bold">1. Adoni-zedek--</hi>"lord of righteousness"--nearly synonymous with Melchizedek, "king of righteousness." These names were common titles of the Jebusite kings.<div eID="gen2782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem--</hi>The original name, "Salem" (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.18">Ge 14:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.76.2">Psa 76:2</reference>), was superseded by that here given, which signifies "a peaceful possession," or "a vision of peace," in allusion, as some think, to the strikingly symbolic scene (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.14">Ge 22:14</reference>) represented on the mount whereon that city was afterwards built.<div eID="gen2783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel, and were among them--</hi>that is, the Israelites; had made an alliance with that people, and acknowledging their supremacy, were living on terms of friendly intercourse with them. <div eID="gen2784" type="x-p"/>
entries.579d01418794c75105942c3e41cdf251ced4869b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2080"/><div sID="gen2785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2080"/><hi type="bold">2. they feared greatly--</hi>The dread inspired by the rapid conquests of the Israelites had been immensely increased by the fact of a state so populous and so strong as Gibeon having found it expedient to submit to the power and the terms of the invaders.<div eID="gen2785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as one of the royal cities--</hi>Although itself a republic (<reference osisRef="Josh.9.3">Jos 9:3</reference>), it was large and well-fortified, like those places in which the chiefs of the country usually established their residence. <div eID="gen2786" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0df618f206c1c1be670ff2411498f5d9be820fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2081"/><div sID="gen2787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2081"/><hi type="bold">3-4. Wherefore Adoni-zedek ... sent, ... saying, Come up unto me, and help me--</hi>A combined attack was meditated on Gibeon, with a view not only to punish its people for their desertion of the native cause, but by its overthrow to interpose a barrier to the farther inroads of the Israelites. This confederacy among the mountaineers of Southern Palestine was formed and headed by the king of Jerusalem, because his territory was most exposed to danger, Gibeon being only six miles distant, and because he evidently possessed some degree of pre-eminence over his royal neighbors. <div eID="gen2787" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc63613e476445a4f1090ecd250c6140c013ed30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2082"/><div sID="gen2788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2082"/><hi type="bold">5. the five kings of the Amorites--</hi>The settlement of this powerful and warlike tribe lay within the confines of Moab; but having also acquired extensive possessions on the southwest of the Jordan, their name, as the ruling power, seems to have been given to the region generally (<reference osisRef="2Sam.21.2">2Sa 21:2</reference>), although Hebron was inhabited by Hittites or Hivites (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.19">Jos 11:19</reference>), and Jerusalem by Jebusites (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.63">Jos 15:63</reference>). <div eID="gen2788" type="x-p"/>
entries.08db69dcdfe42f2a8cab88205cbaed705a65f50f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2083"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.10.6-Josh.10.9">Jos 10:6-9</reference>. Joshua Rescues It.</title> <div sID="gen2789" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2083"/><hi type="bold">6-8. the men of Gibeon sent unto Joshua--</hi>Their appeal was urgent and their claim to protection irresistible, on the ground, not only of kindness and sympathy, but of justice. In attacking the Canaanites, Joshua had received from God a general assurance of success (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.5">Jos 1:5</reference>). But the intelligence of so formidable a combination among the native princes seems to have depressed his mind with the anxious and dispiriting idea that it was a chastisement for the hasty and inconsiderate alliance entered into with the Gibeonites. It was evidently to be a struggle of life and death, not only to Gibeon, but to the Israelites. And in this view the divine communication that was made to him was seasonable and animating. He seems to have asked the counsel of God and received an answer, before setting out on the expedition. <div eID="gen2789" type="x-p"/>
entries.0316743a124904ff927078e3c44838e3151fe4ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2084"/><div sID="gen2790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2084"/><hi type="bold">9. Joshua therefore came upon them suddenly--</hi>This is explained in the following clause, where he is described as having accomplished, by a forced march of picked men, in one night, a distance of twenty-six miles, which, according to the slow pace of Eastern armies and caravans, had formerly been a three days' journey (<reference osisRef="Josh.9.17">Jos 9:17</reference>).<div eID="gen2790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2791" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Josh.10.10">Jos 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.11">11</reference>. God Fights against Them with Hailstones. <div eID="gen2791" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3b0a5097af0d5181e6494ad4150e3729563c617: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2085"/><div sID="gen2792" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2085"/><hi type="bold">10-11. the Lord discomfited them--</hi>Hebrew, "terrified," confounded the Amorite allies, probably by a fearful storm of lightning and thunder. So the word is usually employed (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.10">1Sa 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.13">Psa 18:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.6">144:6</reference>).<div eID="gen2792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and slew them with a great slaughter at Gibeon--</hi>This refers to the attack of the Israelites upon the besiegers. It is evident that there had been much hard fighting around the heights of Gibeon, for the day was far spent before the enemy took to flight.<div eID="gen2793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chased them along the way that goeth up to Beth-horon--</hi>that is, "the House of Caves," of which there are still traces existing. There were two contiguous villages of that name, upper and nether. Upper Beth-horon was nearest Gibeon--about ten miles distant, and approached by a gradual ascent through a long and precipitous ravine. This was the first stage of the flight. The fugitives had crossed the high ridge of Upper Beth-horon, and were in full flight down the descent to Beth-horon the Nether. The road between the two places is so rocky and rugged that there is a path made by means of steps cut in the rock [Robinson]. Down this pass Joshua continued his victorious rout. Here it was that the Lord interposed, assisting His people by means of a storm, which, having been probably gathering all day, burst with such irresistible fury, that "they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword." The Oriental hailstorm is a terrific agent; the hailstones are masses of ice, large as walnuts, and sometimes as two fists; their prodigious size, and the violence with which they fall, make them always very injurious to property, and often fatal to life. The miraculous feature of this tempest, which fell on the Amorite army, was the entire preservation of the Israelites from its destructive ravages. <div eID="gen2794" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef623a72f442c0e07b7c145ab4923b9d338155a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2086"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.10.12-Josh.10.15">Jos 10:12-15</reference>. The Sun and Moon Stand Still at the Word of Joshua.</title> <div sID="gen2795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2086"/><hi type="bold">12-15. Then spake Joshua to the Lord ... and ... he said in the sight of Israel, Sun, stand thou still ... and thou, Moon--</hi>The inspired author here breaks off the thread of his history of this miraculous victory to introduce a quotation from an ancient poem, in which the mighty acts of that day were commemorated. The passage, which is parenthetical, contains a poetical description of the victory which was miraculously gained by the help of God, and forms an extract from "the book of Jasher," that is, "the upright"--an anthology, or collection of national songs, in honor of renowned and eminently pious heroes. The language of a poem is not to be literally interpreted; and therefore, when the sun and moon are personified, addressed as intelligent beings, and represented as standing still, the explanation is that the light of the sun and moon was supernaturally prolonged by the same laws of refraction and reflection that ordinarily cause the sun to appear above the horizon, when it is in reality below it [Keil, Bush]. Gibeon ("a hill") was now at the back of the Israelites, and the height would soon have intercepted the rays of the setting sun. The valley of Ajalon ("stags") was before them, and so near that it was sometimes called "the valley of Gibeon" (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.21">Is 28:21</reference>). It would seem, from <reference osisRef="Josh.10.14">Jos 10:14</reference>, that the command of Joshua was in reality a prayer to God for the performance of this miracle; and that, although the prayers of eminently good men like Moses often prevailed with God, never was there on any other occasion so astonishing a display of divine power made in behalf of His people, as in answer to the prayer of Joshua. <reference osisRef="Josh.10.15">Jos 10:15</reference> is the end of the quotation from Jasher; and it is necessary to notice this, as the fact described in it is recorded in due course, and the same words, by the sacred historian (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.43">Jos 10:43</reference>). <div eID="gen2795" type="x-p"/>
entries.0086c91692a6c2de308f96c5162a43f1c9467b8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2087"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.10.16-Josh.10.27">Jos 10:16-27</reference>. The Five Kings Hanged.</title> <div sID="gen2796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2087"/><hi type="bold">16-27. these five kings ... hid themselves in a cave--</hi>Hebrew, "the cave."<div eID="gen2796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at Makkedah--</hi>The pursuit was continued, without interruption, to Makkedah at the foot of the western mountains, where Joshua seems to have halted with the main body of his troops while a detachment was sent forward to scour the country in pursuit of the remaining stragglers, a few of whom succeeded in reaching the neighboring cities. The last act, probably the next day, was the disposal of the prisoners, among whom the five kings were consigned to the infamous doom of being slain (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.16">De 20:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.17">17</reference>); and then their corpses were suspended on five trees till the evening. <div eID="gen2797" type="x-p"/>
entries.37be200734422400276fa66787dfcb2afa03fef3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2089"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.10.28-Josh.10.42">Jos 10:28-42</reference>. Seven More Kings Conquered.</title> <div sID="gen2799" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2089"/><hi type="bold">28-42. that day Joshua took Makkedah--</hi>In this and the following verses is described the rapid succession of victory and extermination which swept the whole of southern Palestine into the hands of Israel. "All these kings and their land did Joshua take at one time, because the Lord God of Israel fought for Israel. And Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, unto the camp to Gilgal." <chapter eID="Josh.10"/>

entries.94644fdb5a1e937305f39a926bcc142731478439: <div eID="gen7705" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen7706" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7707" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7707" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7706" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7708" type="x-p"/> Adoni-zedec, king of Jerusalem, hearing of the capture of Ai, and that the Gibeonites had made peace with Israel, calls to his assistance four other kings to fight against Gibeon, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.1-Jos.10.4">Jos 10:1-4</reference>. They join forces, and encamp against Gibeon, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.5">Jos 10:5</reference>. The Gibeonites send to Joshua for succor, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.6">Jos 10:6</reference>, who immediately marches to their relief, receives encouragement from God, and falls suddenly on the confederate forces, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.7-Jos.10.9">Jos 10:7-9</reference>, and defeats them; they fly, and multitudes of them are slain by a miraculous shower of hail-stones, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.10">Jos 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.11">Jos 10:11</reference>. Joshua, finding that the day began to fail, prayed that the sun and moon might stand still, that they might have time to pursue and utterly destroy these confederate forces, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.12">Jos 10:12</reference>. The sun and moon stand still, and make that day as long as two, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.13">Jos 10:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.14">Jos 10:14</reference>. Joshua and the people return to their camp at Gilgal, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.15">Jos 10:15</reference>. The five kings having taken shelter in a cave at Makkedah, Joshua commanded the people to roll great stones against the mouth of the cave, and set a watch to keep it, while Israel were pursuing their enemies, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.16-Jos.10.19">Jos 10:16-19</reference>. The Israelites return to Makkedah, bring forth the five kings, then slay and hang them on five trees, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.20-Jos.10.27">Jos 10:20-27</reference>. The Israelites take and destroy Makkedah, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.28">Jos 10:28</reference>, and Libnah, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.29">Jos 10:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.30">Jos 10:30</reference>, and Lachish, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.31">Jos 10:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.32">Jos 10:32</reference>, and defeat Horam king of Gezer, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.33">Jos 10:33</reference>, and take Eglon, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.34">Jos 10:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.35">Jos 10:35</reference>, and Hebron, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.36">Jos 10:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.37">Jos 10:37</reference>, and Debir, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.38">Jos 10:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.39">Jos 10:39</reference>, and all the country of the hills, south, vale, and springs, and the whole country from Kadesh-Barnea to Gibeon, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.40-Jos.10.42">Jos 10:40-42</reference>. They return to Gilgal, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.43">Jos 10:43</reference>. <div eID="gen7708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7709" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen7709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7710" type="x-p"/> Adoni-zedec - This name signifies the Lord of justice or righteousness; and it has been conjectured that the Canaanitish kings assumed this name in imitation of that of the ancient patriarchal king of this city, Melchizedek, whose name signifies king of righteousness, or my righteous king: a supposition that is not improbable, when the celebrity of Melchizedek is considered. <div eID="gen7710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7711" type="x-p"/> Jerusalem - ירושלם Yerushalam. This word has been variously explained; if it be compounded of שלם shalam, peace, perfection, etc., and ראה raah, he saw, it may signify the vision of peace - or, he shall see peace or perfection.
entries.21c57fbf27b57d1241407f974665f18463116a60: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen7711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7712" type="x-p"/> As one of the royal cities - Not a regal city, but great, well inhabited and well fortified, as those cities which served for the royal residence generally were. It does not appear that the Gibeonites had any king - they seem to have been a small but powerful republic, all the men thereof were mighty, merely governed by their elders: for in their address to Joshua, <reference osisRef="Jos.9.11">Jos 9:11</reference>, they mention no king, but simply state that they were sent by their elders and the inhabitants of their country; nor do we any where read of their king; and therefore we may naturally suppose that they had none.
entries.471da62417902687c6663cdbf7ccde74d8f7504c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen7712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7713" type="x-p"/> Hoham king of Hebron - This city was situated in the mountains, southward of Jerusalem, from which it was about thirty miles distant. It fell to the tribe of Judah. <div eID="gen7713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7714" type="x-p"/> Piram king of Jarmuth - There were two cities of this name; one belonged to the tribe of Issachar, see <reference osisRef="Jos.21.29">Jos 21:29</reference>; that mentioned here fell to the tribe of Judah, see <reference osisRef="Jos.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference>; it is supposed to have been about eighteen miles distant from Jerusalem. <div eID="gen7714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7715" type="x-p"/> Japhia king of Lachish - This city is celebrated in Scripture; in that city Amaziah was slain by conspirators, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.19">2Kgs 14:19</reference>. It was besieged by Sennacherib, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14">2Kgs 18:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.17">2Kgs 18:17</reference>; and without effect by the king of Assyria, as we learn from <reference osisRef="Isa.37.8">Isa 37:8</reference> : it was also besieged by the army of Nebuchadnezzar, see <reference osisRef="Jer.34.7">Jer 34:7</reference>; it also fell to the lot of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.39">Jos 15:39</reference>. <div eID="gen7715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7716" type="x-p"/> Debir king of Eglon - Where this city was situated is very uncertain; but we learn from <reference osisRef="Jos.15.39">Jos 15:39</reference>, that it fell to the lot of the tribe of Judah.
entries.b8daeba77317c97014ef038b1894f7b359309cce: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen7716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7717" type="x-p"/> The five kings of the Amorites - This is a general name for the inhabitants of Canaan, otherwise called Canaanites; and it is very likely that they had this appellation because the Amorites were the most powerful tribe or nation in that country. The inhabitants of Jerusalem were Jebusites, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.63">Jos 15:63</reference>; those of Hebron were Hittites, <reference osisRef="Gen.23.2">Gen 23:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.23.3">Gen 23:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.25.9">Gen 25:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.10">Gen 25:10</reference>; and the Gibeonites were Hivites, <reference osisRef="Jos.9.7">Jos 9:7</reference>; and yet all these are called Amorites occasionally, probably for the reason already mentioned, viz., because that tribe was most numerous and powerful.
entries.890645c7458a0ef8365d4b02e0f98e154af535ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen7717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7718" type="x-p"/> Joshua - came unto them suddenly - This he did by a forced march during the night, for he went up from Gilgal all night; from Gilgal to Gibeon was about eighteen or twenty miles; and, having fallen so unexpectedly on these confederate kings, they were immediately thrown into confusion.
entries.ca89ba65d615cc2478b33ed21a79034e9c894ae4: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen7718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7719" type="x-p"/> Slew them with a great slaughter at Gibeon - Multitudes of them fell in the onset; after which they fled, and the Israelites pursued them by the way of Beth-horon. There were two cities of this name, the upper and lower, both in the tribe of Ephraim, and built by Sherah, the daughter of Ephraim, <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.24">1Chr 7:24</reference>. The situation of these two cities is not exactly known. <div eID="gen7719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7720" type="x-p"/> To Azekah, and unto Makkedah - These two cities were in the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.35-Jos.15.41">Jos 15:35-41</reference>.
entries.46fe84863b6013a0cabf448c3bb1d1e144a83f68: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen7720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7721" type="x-p"/> The Lord cast down great stones from heaven upon them - Some have contended that stones, in the common acceptation of the word, are intended here; and that the term hail-stones is only used to point out the celerity of their fall, and their quantity. That stones have fallen from the clouds, if not from a greater height, is a most incontestable fact. That these have fallen in different parts of the world is also true; the East Indies, America, France, Germany, England, Ireland, etc., have all witnessed this phenomenon: of such stones I possess and have seen several fragments; some considerable pieces may be seen in the British Museum. That God might have cast down such stones as these on the Canaanites, there can be no doubt, because his power is unlimited; and the whole account proves that here there was a miraculous interference. But it is more likely that hail-stones, in the proper sense of the word, are meant as well as expressed in the text. That God on other occasions has made use of hail-stones to destroy both men and cattle, we have ample proof in the plague of hail that fell on the Egyptians. See the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.9.18">Exo 9:18</reference>. There is now before me a square of glass, taken out of a south window in the house of Mr. Ball of Crockerton, in the parish of Longbridge Deverell, county of Wilts., through which a hail-stone passed in a shower that fell there June 1, 1780, at two o'clock, P.M. The hole is an obtuse ellipsis or oval, and is cut as true as if it had been done with a diamond: it is three inches and a half in diameter; a proof that the stone that pierced it, which was about eleven inches in circumference, came with inconceivable velocity, else the glass must have been shivered to pieces. I have known a cannon ball go through a square of glass in the cabin window of a ship, and make precisely the same kind of hole, without either shattering or even starring the glass.
